imageUrl.description: Optional: a public image URL to edit instead of the most recently generated image (e.g. one found via getBestImage).

annotations.description: Optional: the exact 'annotations' array from a prior annotateImage call on this same image, to precisely constrain the edit to specific labeled region(s) — only pass the box(es) actually relevant to this instruction, not every box that was detected.

tools.name: generateCarousel
tools.description: Generate a multi-slide image carousel — a consistently-styled set of illustrated slides, each with a headline/body/label overlaid on an AI-generated background — and show it in chat both as a flip-through PDF (page 1 = slide 1, etc.) for reviewing/sharing the whole set as one file, AND as individually downloadable PNGs per slide, since a PDF alone can't actually be posted anywhere a carousel is meant to go (Instagram, LinkedIn, etc. only accept image files). Use this for an Instagram/LinkedIn-carousel-style visual explainer: a listicle, a step-by-step breakdown, a 'top N' post, a short educational sequence — anything that reads as a short series of visually cohesive slides rather than one image or a wall of text. Every slide shares ONE consistent illustration style — the first slide's background is generated fresh from `style` + that slide's own `imagePrompt`, and every later slide reuses the FIRST slide's actual image as a style reference (not just re-describing the style in words again) so the whole deck visually coheres the way a real illustrated series would, instead of drifting slide to slide. Keep `imagePrompt` about the SCENE/SUBJECT only (e.g. 'a lone hiker reaching a mountain summit at sunrise') — the shared `style` covers the artistic treatment (e.g. 'flat minimalist illustration, warm pastel gradient, soft rounded shapes'), so don't repeat style words in every slide's imagePrompt. `headline`/`body`/`label` are rendered as real, sharp overlay text — never described to the image model — so they're always exactly what you wrote, correctly spelled, however long or number-heavy they are; this deliberately avoids asking an image model to render the actual words, since image models are still unreliable at exact, legible multi-word text, and a wrong digit or misspelling baked into pixels is far harder to catch than a bad tool argument. Never ask the background image itself to include text/lettering. Pass `format` to match where this is going: '4:5' for an Instagram feed post (default), '9:16' for Stories/Reels/TikTok, '1:1' for a square post, '16:9' for a landscape/YouTube-style slide. This produces STATIC slides only, no audio or video — if the user also wants it as a narrated video, follow up with generateVideoFromCarousel. The result card has format tabs (4:5 / 9:16 / 1:1 / 16:9) that show this SAME carousel in any shape for free, so always pass the `format` the user asked for (it decides which tab opens first), and never regenerate just to change the format later.

slides.description: 1-8 slides, in display order. A single slide is fine for a one-image post.

headline.description: The slide's main on-screen text — short and punchy.

body.description: Optional smaller supporting text below the headline.

label.description: Optional small uppercase tag above the headline, e.g. 'STEP 1' or 'MYTH'.

imagePrompt.description: The background illustration's subject/scene only — style comes from the shared `style` param, don't repeat it here. Not needed when `imageUrl` is given.

imageUrl.description: Optional: use this photo as the slide's picture instead of generating an illustration — a product image from getShopifyProduct: pass its short `ref` (photo_1, photo_2, …), NOT the long URL (long URLs get corrupted when copied; a wrong character means a 404) — or a `url` from getBestImage, OR an image id (img_N) of one you generated/edited earlier in this conversation (editImage/generateImage; ids from findGeneratedImages). The photo is shown whole (not cropped) with the text beside/below it. Use different photos on different slides, and pick real photographs — skip logos, icons, maps, flags and tiny thumbnails. If you ALSO give imagePrompt, the photo is RE-STAGED by AI instead (so for photos the user wants unedited — 'no AI', 'as is' — give NO imagePrompt): the product is kept as it is and placed in the scene the prompt describes (billed image generation; can subtly alter small details like logos or text). To make real photos 'cooler', PREFER this (imageUrl + imagePrompt on each slide, one call, all slides in parallel) over calling editImage on each photo first — editImage runs one at a time, roughly 30s each. The imagePrompt describes only the SCENE around what the photo already shows — never add a product, tool or part the photo doesn't contain (do NOT ask for a knife in a photo of its pouch: the image model invents a wrong one). Keep the framing of the photo in imagePrompt: for a close-up or detail photo ask for a close-up in a new setting (macro, dramatic lighting), NOT for the whole product — the model invents whatever it can't see. Every re-staged slide is automatically checked against the original photo by a vision model and regenerated (up to 3 attempts) if the product was changed or the scene is poor; the result's `restageChecks` and summary say how each went — report any slide that used the original photo or only partly matched, don't hide it.

restageCloseUp.description: Set true ONLY when the user explicitly asks for AI on a close-up / detail photo (a macro, engraving, texture). By default such photos are kept as the real photo even when you give an imagePrompt, because re-staging a detail shot tends to invent or distort the product.

style.description: Shared artistic style/treatment applied to every slide's background, e.g. 'flat minimalist illustration, warm pastel palette, soft gradients'. Defaults to a plain clean-illustration style if omitted.

font.description: Type style for the on-slide text — ALWAYS choose one to fit the brief's tone: 'serif' for luxury / elegant / premium / editorial / wedding / beauty / heritage; 'condensed' (tall uppercase headlines) for sales / sport / fitness / events / bold poster looks; 'handwritten' for casual / personal / friendly / kids / lifestyle; 'sans' only for neutral, technical or corporate topics. The card has a font picker, so the user can also switch it afterwards for free.

format.description: The shape the user asked for (9:16 for Reels/Stories/TikTok/Shorts) — it decides which tab the result opens on; the user can switch tabs afterwards. Defaults to '4:5'.

tools.name: regenerateCarouselSlide
tools.description: Redo ONE slide of the carousel you just made — e.g. a slide that fell back to the original photo, came out weak or weird, or that the user wants in a different scene — without touching or re-billing the others. Pass the 1-based `slide` number; pass a new `imagePrompt` to change the scene, or omit it to try the same scene again (results vary from run to run, so a plain retry often works). Redoing a slide is an explicit request for AI on it, so this also re-stages a close-up/detail photo that generateCarousel kept as the real photo. Re-staged photo slides go through the same automatic quality check and retries as in generateCarousel. The other slides, the font, the format and any narration are kept as they are. Shows the updated carousel. Each redo is a billed image generation (more if the quality check retries).

slide.description: Which slide to redo, counting from 1.

imagePrompt.description: Optional new scene for this slide. Omit to retry the same scene.

tools.name: removeCarouselSlide
tools.description: Remove one or more slides from the carousel you just made — e.g. the user says a slide is weak, redundant or not wanted ('drop slide 3', 'remove the last two'). Free and instant: nothing is regenerated or re-billed; the remaining slides, the font, the format and their narration are kept, the page numbers update, and the updated carousel is shown. Pass 1-based slide numbers. The last remaining slide can't be removed. Use this instead of calling generateCarousel again. (The user can also remove a slide themselves with the button in the slide viewer.)

slides.description: The slide numbers to remove, counting from 1 in the CURRENT carousel (e.g. [3], or [2,4]).

tools.name: generateVideoFromCarousel
tools.description: Turn the carousel you JUST built with generateCarousel into a narrated video (MP4) — slides on screen, a voice reading over them, each slide shown for exactly as long as its own narration lasts. Use this when the user wants the carousel as a video / reel / presentation / voiceover rather than (or in addition to) still images. It always operates on the most recent generateCarousel result in this conversation, so call generateCarousel first (its format decides the video's shape: 4:5, 9:16 for Reels/Shorts/TikTok, 1:1 or 16:9); if there isn't one yet, this returns an error. Provide `narration`: an array with exactly ONE string per slide, in order, written to be SPOKEN in the SAME language as the slides' on-screen text (never the UI or browser language — the voice reads it verbatim, so French narration over English slides is a mismatch) — conversational, and short (roughly 15-40 words per slide; a slide is on screen only as long as its narration takes). Don't just read the on-slide headline back word for word; say what a presenter would say over it, and let the last one wrap up. If you omit `narration`, each slide's own headline and body are read aloud as-is (fine as a quick draft, flatter than a written script). Optional `voice` (a Gemini prebuilt voice name, e.g. "Kore", "Charon", "Zephyr", "Orus") and `style` (delivery direction such as 'upbeat and energetic' or 'calm, warm, unhurried') apply to every slide, so the whole video sounds like one presenter. This is slow and costs credits (one text-to-speech call per slide, run in parallel, then an in-browser video encode; expect roughly 20-60 seconds and a one-time download of the encoder the first time) — only call it when the user actually asked for a video, not as an automatic follow-up to every carousel.

narration.description: Exactly one spoken script per slide, in slide order, in the same language as the slides' on-screen text. Omit to read each slide's own headline + body instead.

voice.description: Optional Gemini prebuilt voice name applied to every slide, e.g. Kore, Charon, Zephyr, Orus.

style.description: Optional delivery direction applied to every slide, e.g. 'upbeat and energetic'.

format.description: Optional video shape; defaults to the carousel's own format. The video card also has format tabs the user can switch between, so only pass this when they asked for a specific shape. Calling again with just a different format reuses the existing narration (no new speech).

tools.name: annotateImage
tools.description: Detect and label the distinct objects/areas in an image, and show it in chat with numbered boxes drawn over each one (labels are listed below the image, not drawn on it, to avoid clutter). This is a cheap vision call, not the image-generation model — not a billed generation, so it's fine to call before writing a precise editImage instruction, e.g. when the user says 'remove the thing on the left' and you don't yet know exactly what's there or where. Pass the returned annotations array straight into editImage's `annotations` param to ground that edit to the right region. By default annotates the most recently generated/edited image in this conversation; pass imageUrl to annotate a real photo from the web instead (e.g. one found via getBestImage).

imageUrl.description: Optional: a public image URL to annotate instead of the most recently generated/edited image.

tools.name: generateSpeech
tools.description: Generate real spoken-word audio from the `lines` you give and show it in chat as a playable audio clip — narration by one voice, or a natural conversation between up to 4 distinct named speakers (each gets its own consistent voice throughout). Handles a full-length piece in one call — a whole short story, a 15-20 minute two-person podcast-style episode — not just a short clip: the lines are split into chunks and every chunk's generation runs concurrently, then stitched into one MP3, the same approach and format reloadium-podcasts itself uses for full episodes. Use for something worth actually hearing performed well. Not a substitute for the quiz tool's free built-in read-aloud (that's for reading one sentence, not a real generation). Each call is a real, billed generation — don't call it speculatively, and don't split a long piece into multiple separate generateSpeech calls yourself, since that adds unnecessary round-trips for no benefit — pass all the lines in one call, up to the length limit stated in the error if you somehow exceed it.

lines.description: The script, in order, as an array of turns: [{"speaker":"Alex","text":"..."}, {"speaker":"Sam","text":"..."}]. For single-voice narration omit `speaker`: [{"text":"..."}]. Up to 4 distinct speaker names. Keep each entry to roughly 15 seconds of spoken audio (~40 words) or less — real dialogue is short back-and-forth turns, not monologues; split a longer thought into consecutive same-speaker entries instead of one long one.

speaker.description: Character/speaker name. Up to 4 distinct names across the whole script.

text.description: One turn — aim for ~40 words/15 seconds of speech or less, even for narration. Continue a longer thought as another entry with the same speaker rather than one long block.

voices.description: Optional: explicit {speakerName: voiceName} overrides. Omitted speakers get an automatically assigned voice, kept consistent for that speaker across the whole script.

style.description: Optional tone/delivery direction, e.g. 'calm and reassuring', 'energetic and playful, like two witty friends chatting'.

tools.name: webSearch
tools.description: Search the web with Google for current or external information — news, prices, recent events, live data, anything time-sensitive or that you can't be confident about — and get back a written answer with its sources. Use it instead of guessing or saying you lack real-time access, then write your reply (or your next tool call, e.g. turning the findings into audio or a carousel) from what it returns. Its sources are general pages the answer drew on, not verified links to a specific business or product — for those use findRealLinks. It is a separate billed search call, so ask one well-formed question per call.

query.description: What to find out, phrased as a specific question or topic (e.g. 'good news from Krakow in the past two weeks').

tools.name: findRealLinks
tools.description: Search the web and get back Brave's own list of results — each with its real title, URL and snippet as the page itself gives them, so a title and its link always belong together. Use it to find or confirm a genuine URL for something specific (a business's website, an official ticket page, a product page, docs, a video), not for general current-events questions — use webSearch for those. Pass type "videos" when the user wants videos (results then come from video search, with creator and duration). It does not check that a result is the exact thing the user named: pick a result only when its title/site clearly is that item, and say so when nothing is. One query per call (2 credits); phrase it as a normal search query.

query.description: What to search for — be specific (e.g. 'Noma restaurant Copenhagen official website' rather than just 'Noma').

count.description: Max results to return, 1-10. Defaults to 5.

tools.name: verifyInText
tools.description: Check whether specific text genuinely appears — verbatim, or as a reverse complement for a DNA/RNA sequence — inside a longer source text, and get its real character position. Use this instead of trusting your own read of where something appears in a long document or sequence: locating exact positions within long text is an easy thing to get subtly wrong, unlike arithmetic on numbers you already have — once you have verified positions from this tool, computing a span/distance between them yourself is reliable, so don't call this a second time just to redo that subtraction. Examples: does a quote/clause actually appear in a document the user pasted (and where), does a claimed error string actually appear in a log dump, does a PCR primer's binding site actually exist in a DNA template. Case-sensitive exact match. Set reverseComplement:true on an item to search for its DNA/RNA reverse complement instead of the sequence itself — this is how a reverse PCR primer actually binds its template, not verbatim.

source.description: The longer text or sequence to search within.

items.description: 1 or more things to verify against source.

text.description: The exact text/sequence to look for.

reverseComplement.description: DNA/RNA only: search for this sequence's reverse complement instead of itself.

tools.name: generatePdf
tools.description: Generate a real, downloadable, paginated PDF document from structured content and show it in chat — for a report, a comparison writeup, an itinerary, or anything the user wants to save/print/share outside the chat, not for a quick answer that reads fine as a normal message. Free and instant (runs entirely in the browser, not a billed generation) — fine to call whenever a proper document is genuinely useful, but don't reach for it just to restate something a normal reply already covers. Provide `title` and `sections`, each {heading?, paragraphs?: string[], bulletList?: string[], table?: {headers: string[], rows: string[][]}, chart?: {...}, graph?: {...}, gauge?: {...}, map?: {...}} — mix and match per section as needed (a section can have a heading plus paragraphs, or just a table, etc.). Pagination and text wrapping are handled automatically. Text renders in a real Unicode font, so French/German/Spanish/Polish/Turkish accented characters are safe to use directly. A section's optional `chart` takes the exact same shape as showChart's own args (type/data/series/unit/title/links/xLabel/yLabel — see showChart's own description for the full per-type shapes) — if you already called showChart earlier in this conversation and want that same chart included in the PDF, pass the identical args again here rather than re-describing the data as a table. A section's optional `graph` takes the exact same shape as showGraph's own args (nodes/edges/layout/title — see showGraph's own description) for embedding a network/dependency diagram instead. A section's optional `gauge` takes the exact same shape as showGauge's own args (value/min/max/unit/label/zones/title) for embedding a single score/metric dial instead. A section's optional `map` takes the exact same shape as showMap's own args (pins/route/title — see showMap's own description) for embedding a static map with pins and any route instead — it's a static snapshot, not interactive, so it needs the pins actually spread out visually to be worth including. All four are always rendered light-themed regardless of the chat's current theme, since the PDF is meant to be read/printed outside the app. The same unit-consistency rules from showChart apply to `chart` (don't mix a dollar total with a percentage in one chart) — a chart embedded in a PDF is exactly as unreadable when units are mixed as one shown in chat.

chart.description: Same shape as showChart's args — see that tool's description.

graph.description: Same shape as showGraph's args — see that tool's description.

gauge.description: Same shape as showGauge's args — see that tool's description.

map.description: Same shape as showMap's args — see that tool's description.

tools.name: generateFacturXInvoice
tools.description: Generate a real, downloadable Factur-X/ZUGFeRD-compliant e-invoice (a PDF/A-3b document with a machine-readable CII XML invoice embedded inside it, per the EN 16931 BASIC profile) and show it in chat. Use this specifically when the user wants an actual compliant e-invoice to send to a client or submit through French/German e-invoicing systems — not for a generic-looking invoice/quote as a normal document (use generatePdf for that; it's simpler and doesn't force the strict Factur-X data shape). Runs entirely in the browser, free and instant. All monetary amounts are numbers in the invoice's own currency (not strings, not pre-formatted). Every line item needs its own VAT rate — don't assume they're all the same. Line totals, VAT breakdown, and grand total are computed automatically from quantity × unitPrice per line; don't pass totals yourself. Country codes are 2-letter ISO 3166-1 (e.g. 'FR', 'DE'); currency is a 3-letter ISO 4217 code (e.g. 'EUR'). issueDate/dueDate are 'YYYY-MM-DD'. `language` only changes the visible page's labels (SELLER/BILL TO, table headers, totals) to match — the embedded XML's element names are always the same fixed UN/CEFACT English tags, in every Factur-X invoice, regardless of language; that's not a bug to work around.

currency.description: 3-letter ISO 4217 code, e.g. 'EUR'.

language.description: ISO 639-1 code for the visible page's labels: 'en' (default), 'fr', 'de', 'es', 'tr', or 'pl'. Match the user's own language unless they ask otherwise.

vatId.description: e.g. 'FR12345678901' — optional but expected for a real invoice.

unitCode.description: UN/CEFACT Rec 20 unit code — default 'C62' (piece/each) if unsure.

unitPrice.description: Per-unit price excl. VAT, in the invoice currency.

vatRatePercent.description: e.g. 20, 10, 5.5, 2.1, or 0 for this specific line.

notes.description: Optional free-text notes (payment terms, references, etc.).

tools.name: extractInfoFromCV
tools.description: Extract a candidate's real background from CV/resume text into clean structured data (name, contact, experience, education, skills, certifications) — call this FIRST whenever you're about to build a resume from an attached or pasted CV, especially before generateOptimizedResume, instead of re-reading and re-interpreting the free text yourself each time. This runs a separate, narrowly-scoped extraction pass with no tailoring pressure, so it only pulls out what's literally stated — nothing inferred or embellished. Pass its skills[] straight through as generateOptimizedResume's own sourceSkills argument: that tool checks its output against it and rejects anything that isn't actually there, so extracting first and reusing this result is how you avoid — not just try to avoid — inventing a skill the person doesn't have. Also the right first step from the OTHER side of the table — a recruiter deciding whether to move forward with a candidate. Full sequence, all four steps, not a subset: (1) extract the candidate's resume here, (2) fetch the job posting with getPageMarkdown, (3) call showChart with a 'radar' plotting TWO series on the role's key axes — the candidate's real, extracted competency level on each, and a 'Required' series for what the role actually needs there, never the candidate alone with nothing to measure it against, (4) call showProsCons for the actual weighted decision. Steps 3 and 4 answer different questions — the radar shows the SHAPE of the fit, showProsCons WEIGHS it into a recommendation — so do both, not whichever one you reach first; stopping after the radar (or after a prose opinion with neither) leaves the question technically unanswered even if your text sounds conclusive. Cheap vision/text call, not a full generation. That four-step sequence is for ONE candidate. When more than one candidate's CV/resume is attached for the SAME role, call this tool once per CV — each call is independent and just as cheap — then fetch the posting once with getPageMarkdown, and replace step 4 with a single showComparisonMatrix call instead of a per-candidate showProsCons: the role's key requirements as dimensions, one option per candidate, each scored only from what that candidate's own extraction actually shows — that ranking, not a repeated yes/no, is what answers 'which of these should I move forward with'. Up to 3 candidates total, ALSO do step 3 — don't drop it just because you already showed the matrix: call showChart 'radar' overlaying each candidate against a 'Required' series on the same axes, reusing the exact per-dimension scores you just gave showComparisonMatrix rather than re-scoring (same as showChart's own radar/matrix-reuse guidance describes) — the matrix ranks them, the radar shows WHY, in shape, and a recommendation with only one of the two is incomplete the same way stopping after only the radar or only showProsCons is in the single-candidate case above. Only beyond 3 candidates does the radar stop being an option (too many overlaid polygons to read) and the matrix alone is the complete answer.

cvText.description: The CV/resume's full text — the markdown already extracted from an attached document, or text the user pasted directly.

tools.name: generateOptimizedResume
tools.description: Generate a clean, single-column, ATS-safe resume PDF from the user's real background and show it in chat. Renders via the exact same engine as generatePdf (single column, standard section headers, one embedded Unicode font, no tables/columns/text-boxes/icons) since those are precisely the layout patterns that break real ATS parsers (Workday, Greenhouse, iCIMS, Lever) — you don't need to think about formatting, just supply clean structured content. If the user gives you a job posting URL, call getPageMarkdown on it FIRST and use the real result — don't call this tool claiming to have tailored the resume to a posting you haven't actually fetched and read, that's a false claim even if the resume still looks reasonable. When there's a target role or job posting to tailor against, call useStrongerModel with {"stronger":true} before this tool: telling genuine tailoring apart from fabrication takes real judgment under pressure to match the posting's keywords, and getting it wrong here means a factually false resume, not just a formatting slip — the same trade-off useStrongerModel's own description asks you to weigh. A plain resume with no target role to match doesn't need it. Once there's a target role or job posting in this conversation (fetched via getPageMarkdown, or described by the user), tailor the summary and bullet wording to genuinely and naturally reflect that role's real terminology and priorities — but ONLY using the user's actual, already-known background; never invent skills, employers, titles, or achievements they haven't told you about. This includes the skills[] list specifically: only put a technology/skill there if the source material explicitly says the person has used, studied, or worked with it — inferring a specific unlisted technology from a same-domain but different thing (e.g. listing 'Go' because they took a 'Performance Engineering' course, or 'SQL/MySQL' because the target role wants it and they mention 'databases' generically) is fabrication, not tailoring, even though it's exactly the kind of gap-filling that's tempting when a job posting's top requirements don't quite match what someone actually knows. If their real skills don't include something the target role wants, leave it out rather than inventing it — the resume should make their real, honest fit for the role as clear and well-matched as possible, not manufacture a false one. Quantify achievements with real numbers wherever the user's own info supports it (e.g. "cut deploy time from 40min to 6min", "led a team of 5"), since concrete metrics are what both ATS ranking and human reviewers respond to — but don't fabricate a number that isn't grounded in what you actually know. Never use invisible/hidden text, tiny/white-on-white keyword stuffing, or incoherent keyword lists — these are actively detected as fraud signals by real ATS platforms now (confirmed for Workday/Greenhouse/Lever) and by resume-screening LLMs, and get resumes rejected rather than ranked higher. The honest version of 'optimized' is: accurately described, well-matched to the role, and readable — not gamed. If you're building this from an attached or pasted CV, call extractInfoFromCV on its text first and pass its skills[] output straight through as sourceSkills here, unmodified — this tool checks every entry in your own skills[] output against sourceSkills and rejects the whole call if one isn't actually there, so extracting first is how you avoid inventing a skill, not just a rule to remember. When this was tailored against a specific job posting (targetRole/getPageMarkdown were used), don't stop once the PDF is shown — the person still doesn't know how it actually lands with a real reviewer. Immediately continue in the same turn as if you were now the recruiter screening this exact resume against that exact posting: extractInfoFromCV on the markdown you just produced (its content, not the original CV, since that's the version actually being submitted), a showChart 'radar' comparing it to the role's key axes, then showProsCons for the actual verdict — the same full sequence showProsCons's own description asks for, just run for the user's benefit this time instead of a recruiter's. Present the result as feedback, not a verdict on the person: frame any remaining gap as something to check against their real background — 'a recruiter would likely flag missing X — if you've actually done that and it just isn't on your CV yet, tell me and I'll fold it in' — since a gap here often means the original CV under-sold them rather than that they lack the experience. Skip this follow-up entirely for a plain resume with no target role — it's only worth the extra calls when there's a specific posting to be screened against.

contactLine.description: One line: email • phone • city, country • linkedin/portfolio URL — whatever the user actually gave you.

targetRole.description: The role/job posting this is tailored for, if any — for your own context when writing summary/bullets, not necessarily rendered verbatim.

summary.description: Optional 2-4 sentence professional summary, tailored to targetRole if given.

bullets.description: Achievement bullets — quantified where you genuinely know the numbers, never invented.

skills.description: Flat list of real skills the user actually has — matched to the target role's terminology where genuinely applicable, not padded.

sourceSkills.description: extractInfoFromCV's own skills[] output, passed through unmodified — used to verify skills[] above doesn't add anything not actually there. Omit only if you didn't extract from a CV (e.g. the user described their background directly in chat).

tools.name: addToCalendar
tools.description: Add a single event to the user's Google Calendar and show it in chat, with a link back to the real event once created. Use when the user asks to add/save something specific to their calendar (an event you found via findRealLinks, a meeting, a deadline) — not for anything recurring (one-shot events only); use getCalendarEvents instead if the user's asking what's already on their calendar rather than adding something. The first use of ANY calendar tool in a session needs the user to grant access via a one-tap connect card rendered in chat — that access is session-only (never stored beyond the current tab) and shared with getCalendarEvents (one grant covers both), so don't imply it 'remembers' this for later; if the user wants standing calendar access that works across sessions, tell them that's not supported yet rather than guessing. Always pass a real timeZone (an IANA name like 'Europe/Paris') — use the one from the user's own message context block, don't guess or default to UTC.

endDateTime.description: ISO 8601. For an all-day-ish item with no clear end, default to 1 hour after start.

timeZone.description: IANA time zone, e.g. 'Europe/Paris' — from the user's own message context, not guessed.

tools.name: getCalendarEvents
tools.description: Look up what's actually on the user's Google Calendar within a date range and show it in chat. Use when the user asks what they have going on, whether they're free at a time, or to check for conflicts before proposing something — don't guess or say you can't access their calendar without trying this first. Shares its access grant with addToCalendar (one connect covers both) — session-only, never stored. Always pass real ISO timeMin/timeMax computed from the user's own message context (their current date/time), not guessed; defaults to the next 7 days from now if omitted.

timeMin.description: ISO 8601 start of range. Defaults to now.

timeMax.description: ISO 8601 end of range. Defaults to 7 days after timeMin.

tools.name: compareImages
tools.description: Show two images side by side in an interactive comparison widget (slider, split view, or either image alone) — for comparing two DIFFERENT photos or images, not for showing an edit's own before/after (editImage already displays that automatically). Use this for things like comparing two products found via getBestImage, two design options, or a photo the user attached against a reference photo found on the web. Pass a public image URL for each side (e.g. from getBestImage) — fetched server-side, so it works regardless of the source site's CORS policy. Omit one side's URL only to compare a URL against the most recently generated/edited image in this chat.

imageUrl1.description: Public URL of the first / left-hand image. Omit only to use the most recently generated or edited image in this chat.

imageUrl2.description: Public URL of the second / right-hand image. Omit only to use the most recently generated or edited image in this chat.

label.description: Optional short caption describing the comparison, e.g. 'iPhone 15 vs iPhone 16'.

defaultView.description: Which tab the widget opens on — the user can still switch afterward. Use 'slider' when both images share the same subject/composition so a wipe reveal is meaningful (e.g. two angles of the same object). Use 'side' (split view) when the two images are of different, unrelated subjects that don't visually align — e.g. two different products or landmarks. Defaults to 'side' if omitted.

tools.name: generateQrCode
tools.description: Generate a QR code image encoding a URL, Wi-Fi network, contact card, or any short text, and show it in the chat. Generated entirely in the browser — no external service is contacted. For Wi-Fi, encode `WIFI:T:WPA;S:<ssid>;P:<password>;;` (use `T:nopass;` if there's no password). For a contact, encode a vCard string.

data.description: The text, URL, Wi-Fi string, or vCard to encode.

label.description: Optional short caption shown above the QR code.

tools.name: listApps
tools.description: List all available Reloadium apps with their names, categories, descriptions, and URLs. Use this to discover what apps exist before calling openApp.

category.description: Optional category filter: Productivity, Finance, Media, Shopping, Social, Utilities, Audit.

tools.name: searchApps
tools.description: Search for Reloadium apps by keyword, name, or use-case description. Returns matching apps with URLs.

query.description: Search term — app name, keyword, or description of what you want to do.

tools.name: openApp
tools.description: Navigate to a Reloadium app by its ID or name. Call listApps or searchApps first if you're not sure of the exact ID. Pass an optional 'task' string to automatically run a task in the destination app as soon as it loads — use this to chain work across apps (e.g. open Podcasts and tell it to generate a podcast about Rome).

id.description: App ID (e.g. 'reloadium-news') or app name (e.g. 'News'). Case-insensitive.

task.description: Optional instruction to execute automatically in the destination app after it loads. The full conversation history carries over so the destination app has complete context.

tools.name: highlightElement
tools.description: Highlight one or more DOM elements with a pulsing ring so the user can see what the assistant is referring to. Accepts any CSS selector. Scrolls the first match into view. Auto-clears after durationMs (default 4000ms; pass 0 to keep until clearHighlights is called). IMPORTANT: if the element is inside a collapsed accordion or hidden panel (e.g. a recipe phase that is not expanded), it will have zero dimensions and the highlight will be invisible. In that case, first use clickElement on the accordion toggle (e.g. '[data-phase-index="2"] button') to expand it, then call highlightElement on the content inside.

selector.description: CSS selector to match elements, e.g. '.save-button', '#trip-name', '[data-day-id]'.

label.description: Optional tooltip text shown above each highlighted element.

color.description: Optional hex color for the highlight ring, e.g. '#f59e0b'. Defaults to indigo (#6366f1).

durationMs.description: How long (ms) to keep the highlight. Default 4000. Pass 0 to keep until clearHighlights is called.

tools.name: clearHighlights
tools.description: Remove all active UI highlights added by highlightElement.

tools.name: clickElement
tools.description: Click a DOM element on the page identified by a CSS selector. Use this to open panels, toggle accordions, select tabs, or trigger any button or link. Scrolls the element into view before clicking. After clicking an accordion or panel toggle, pass waitMs (default 300) to wait for the CSS transition before the next tool call. Returns what was clicked, how many elements matched, and a warning if multiple matched.

selector.description: CSS selector for the element to click, e.g. '[data-phase-index="2"] button', '[data-conv-id="abc"]'.

waitMs.description: Milliseconds to wait after clicking before returning (default 300). Useful when clicking accordion toggles so CSS transitions finish before you call highlightElement. Pass 0 to return immediately.

tools.name: typeInElement
tools.description: Type text into an input or textarea on the page. Works with React-controlled inputs by firing the native input event that React listens to. Optionally appends to existing content instead of replacing it. Returns what was typed and the element's label.

selector.description: CSS selector for the input or textarea, e.g. 'textarea', '#search-input', '[data-testid="city-input"]'.

text.description: The text to type into the field.

append.description: If true, append to the existing value instead of replacing it. Default false.

pressEnter.description: If true, dispatch a keydown Enter event after typing. Useful for search inputs or chat inputs that submit on Enter. Default false.

tools.name: getHighlightableElements
tools.description: Return a list of meaningful DOM elements on the current page that can be targeted by highlightElement. Each entry includes the best CSS selector, a human-readable label, the element type, and a 'visible' boolean. visible=false means the element is in the DOM but has zero dimensions (e.g. inside a collapsed accordion) — use clickElement on its toggle/header first to expand it before highlighting.

filter.description: Optional keyword to filter elements by their label, role, or selector (e.g. 'save', 'phase').

role.description: Filter to elements matching this exact ARIA role (e.g. 'button', 'tab', 'input', 'link', 'dialog'). More precise than using filter.

visibleOnly.description: If true, return only visible elements. If false, return only hidden/collapsed elements (useful for finding things inside closed accordions). Omit to return all.

limit.description: Maximum number of elements to return. Default 80.

offset.description: Zero-based index of the first element to return. Use with limit for pagination.

tools.name: getPageImages
tools.description: Return all images on the current page: elements, , inline

filter.description: Keyword to filter images by alt text, src URL, or selector (case-insensitive).

kind.description: Return only images of this type. Omit for all.

visibleOnly.description: If true, return only images with non-zero dimensions currently on screen. If false, return only hidden ones. Omit to return all.

includeBackgrounds.description: If false, skip elements whose image comes from a CSS background-image. Default true.

tools.name: listIndexedDB
tools.description: List all IndexedDB databases in the current origin and their object store names. Use this first to discover what data is stored before querying or modifying it.

tools.name: queryIndexedDB
tools.description: Get records from an IndexedDB object store with pagination. Records are sorted newest-first when a 'date', 'createdAt', or 'timestamp' field exists. Returns { records, total, offset, limit, hasMore } so you can page through large stores.

offset.description: Zero-based index of the first record to return. Default 0.

limit.description: Maximum number of records to return per page. Default 20.

tools.name: putIndexedDBRecord
tools.description: Insert or update a single record in an IndexedDB object store. The record must include the store's keyPath field. For out-of-line key stores (no keyPath), supply the key separately via the 'key' parameter. Use queryIndexedDB first to inspect the store's record shape — out-of-line key stores return a '_key' field on each record.

record.description: The record to insert or update. Must include the keyPath field for in-line key stores.

key.description: Out-of-line key to use when the store has no keyPath (e.g. an episode ID string). Omit for stores that have a keyPath.

tools.name: deleteIndexedDBRecord
tools.description: Delete a single record from an IndexedDB object store by its key.

key.description: The key of the record to delete (string, number, or array for compound keys)

tools.name: clearIndexedDBStore
tools.description: Delete ALL records from an IndexedDB object store. Irreversible — use with caution.

tools.name: readCurrentSeries
tools.description: Returns the currently loaded podcast series: title, topic, description, language, and episode list with ids, titles, and audioReady status. Use this to understand what is currently displayed, and to check how many episodes have or lack audio without calling selectEpisode per episode.

tools.name: listSeriesHistory
tools.description: Returns all podcast series saved in history (user-created and demos), with id, title, topic, episodeCount, language, and createdAt.

tools.name: readEpisodeContent
tools.description: Returns the generated content summary for a specific episode: keyFacts, timelineEventCount, quizQuestionCount, transcriptLineCount, and language. The episode must have been selected/generated first.

tools.name: generateSeries
tools.description: Generates a new podcast series outline for the given topic. The app switches to the series view automatically.

topic.description: The podcast topic.

language.description: Language code for episode content, e.g. "en", "fr", "de", "es", "pl". Defaults to "en".

tools.name: loadSeriesFromHistory
tools.description: Loads a previously saved series by id. Use listSeriesHistory to find available series ids.

tools.name: selectEpisode
tools.description: Selects an episode in the current series, triggering content generation if not already cached. Use readCurrentSeries to get episode ids.

tools.name: playEpisodeAudio
tools.description: Plays existing audio for an episode. Call this when audioReady is true after selectEpisode. If audioReady is false, call generateEpisodeAudio instead.

episodeId.description: Episode id. Defaults to the currently selected episode.

tools.name: generateEpisodeAudio
tools.description: Generates TTS audio for an episode and starts playback. Only call this if audioReady was false in the selectEpisode result. If audioReady was true, use playEpisodeAudio instead. The episode content must be generated first (select it). Uses the currently selected episode if no episodeId is provided.

episodeId.description: Optional episode id. Defaults to the currently selected episode.

tools.name: generateAllMissingAudio
tools.description: Bulk-generates TTS audio for all episodes that have content but no audio yet. Fire-and-forget — the UI shows progress automatically. Use when the user wants to generate audio for the entire series at once.

tools.name: generateMoreEpisodes
tools.description: Generates additional episodes for the currently loaded podcast series and appends them to the episode list. Suggest this when the user asks for more episodes or reaches the last episode.

tools.name: controlAudio
tools.description: Controls the audio player at the top of the screen. Use action 'pause' to pause, 'resume' to resume, 'stop' to stop and close the player, 'skipForward' to skip 30 seconds ahead, 'skipBackward' to rewind 30 seconds.

action.description: The playback action to perform.

tools.name: selectEpisodeTab
tools.description: Switches the active tab in the episode view. Available tabs: cover, transcript, timeline, facts, quiz, perspectives.

tools.name: backToStart
tools.description: Navigates back to the topic input screen, clearing the current series and episode selection.

tools.name: generateAllMissingContent
tools.description: Bulk-generates episode content (transcripts, key facts, etc.) for all episodes in the current series that don't have content yet. Fire-and-forget — the UI shows progress. Use when the user wants all episodes ready.

tools.name: deleteSeries
tools.description: Deletes a podcast series from history. If it is the currently loaded series, the view resets to the start screen.

seriesId.description: The id of the series to delete. Use listSeriesHistory to find it.

tools.name: generateSeriesFromUrl
tools.description: Fetches a public URL and generates a full podcast series from its content. Use instead of generateSeries when the user provides a URL. Awaits completion.

url.description: The public URL to fetch and generate a series from.

tools.name: seekAudio
tools.description: Seeks the audio player to a specific time in seconds. Use to jump to a timestamp the user mentions (e.g. '2 minutes 30 seconds' → 150).

tools.name: showPostAttachment
tools.description: Bring something attached to a forum post or comment back into this chat: one of its WIDGETS (shown as the same interactive card), one of its PICTURES (shown here, and you then see the picture itself rather than its one-line description) or one of its PDFs (the user gets a link to it and you get its text). getPost lists what a post and each of its comments has, in order — `widgets`, `pictures`, `files` — and `index` is the position in that list, starting at 0. Use it when the user asks to see, show again or bring back an attachment, and whenever answering needs you to actually look at a picture or read a PDF. A long PDF comes in pieces: call again with `offset` to read on.

post.description: The post id, or its url like /forums/homelab/<id>.

comment.description: Only for something attached to a COMMENT: that comment's id (or its url ending in #comment-<id>). Leave out for the post's own attachments.

index.description: Position in the list getPost gave, starting at 0. Default 0.

offset.description: PDF only: character to start reading from, to continue a long one.

length.description: PDF only: how many characters to read (default 10000).

tools.name: filterByCategory
tools.description: Filter the launcher to show only apps in a specific category. Use 'all' to show everything.

category.description: Category name or 'all', 'favorites', 'mostFrequent'.

tools.name: toggleFavorite
tools.description: Star or unstar an app to add/remove it from the Favorites section.

tools.name: listCategories
tools.description: List all available category filters, including special ones like Favorites and Most Frequent.

tools.name: clearSearch
tools.description: Clear the current search query and show all apps.

tools.name: debugInfo
tools.description: Return runtime environment info to help diagnose loading errors: build hash (from the JS bundle filename), browser UA, localStorage keys, ref population status, and any launcher-specific globals. Use this if the app throws initialization errors or behaves unexpectedly.

tools.name: listFavorites
tools.description: List all apps the user has starred as favorites, sorted alphabetically.

tools.name: listMostRecent
tools.description: List apps the user has launched recently, sorted by most recently launched first.

limit.description: Maximum number of apps to return. Defaults to 10.

tools.name: listMostFrequent
tools.description: List the apps the user launches most often, sorted by launch count descending.

limit.description: Maximum number of apps to return. Defaults to 10.

tools.name: listResults
tools.description: List the apps currently shown on screen after applying the active search query and category filter. Use this to see what the user is looking at right now.

tools.name: readCurrentProject
tools.description: Returns the currently active image editing project: name, description, history count, and the current (latest) image's prompt and edit type. Returns an error if no project is selected.

tools.name: listProjects
tools.description: Returns all image editing projects (id, name, description, history count). Use setActiveProject to switch between them.

tools.name: setActiveProject
tools.description: Switches to a different project by its ID. Use listProjects first to get valid project IDs.

projectId.description: The project ID to activate

tools.name: setEditPrompt
tools.description: Sets the edit prompt text field. Describe the image transformation to apply (e.g. 'Make the background a sunny beach', 'Add a red hat to the person').

prompt.description: Editing instructions for the image

tools.name: setNegativePrompt
tools.description: Sets the negative prompt — elements to avoid in the generated image (e.g. 'blurry, watermark, text').

tools.name: setEditStrength
tools.description: Sets how strongly the edit prompt transforms the original image. 0 = preserve original almost entirely, 100 = full generation (ignore original). Values under 33 use inpainting, 33-67 use img2img, 68-100 use more aggressive generation.

strength.description: Edit strength (0–100)

tools.name: searchProjects
tools.description: Filters the projects list by name. Set to empty string to show all projects.

query.description: Search query to filter projects by name

tools.name: listPresets
tools.description: Returns all available image editing presets — both built-in (loaded from server) and custom (user-created, stored in IndexedDB). Includes label, prompt, optional reference image URL, and optional mode.

tools.name: setActivePreset
tools.description: Activates a preset by label. Use listPresets first to get valid labels. Pass null to clear the active preset.

label.description: Preset label to activate, or null to clear

tools.name: createCustomPreset
tools.description: Creates a new custom preset and saves it to IndexedDB. It will appear first in the preset row.

label.description: Short display name for the preset

prompt.description: The editing prompt to apply

tools.name: deleteCustomPreset
tools.description: Deletes a custom preset by label from IndexedDB.

label.description: Label of the custom preset to delete

tools.name: getCurrentTrip
tools.description: Return the full details of the trip currently open in the planner, including all days, transports, activities, and accommodations. Returns null if no trip is open.

tools.name: listTrips
tools.description: Return a summary list of all saved trips ordered by creation date (newest first). Each entry includes id, name, origin, destination, transport mode, dates, and day count.

tools.name: getTripDetails
tools.description: Return the full details of a specific saved trip by its id.

tools.name: getGeneratingTrips
tools.description: Return the IDs of all trips currently being generated by AI. Useful to check generation status.

tools.name: openTrip
tools.description: Open a specific saved trip in the planner view by its id.

tools.name: goToNewTrip
tools.description: Navigate to the trip creation form so the user can start a new trip.

tools.name: openHistory
tools.description: Open the saved trips history modal.

tools.name: closeHistory
tools.description: Close the saved trips history modal.

tools.name: generateTrip
tools.description: Start generating a new AI trip plan. The trip will appear immediately in the planner with a loading skeleton, and generation runs in the background. Returns the new trip id.

destination.description: Destination city or address (e.g. 'Tokyo').

mode.description: Primary transport mode for the trip.

tripType.description: Whether the trip is one-way or round-trip.

tools.name: deleteTrip
tools.description: Delete a saved trip by its id. Cannot be undone.

tools.name: clearAllTrips
tools.description: Delete all saved trips. Cannot be undone.

tools.name: estimateGenerateTrip
tools.description: Estimate the credit cost to generate a full AI trip plan. Returns { realistic, min, max } credit counts.

destination.description: Destination city (e.g. 'Tokyo').

tools.name: estimateGenerateTripName
tools.description: Estimate the credit cost to generate a short poetic trip name. Returns { realistic, min, max } credit counts.

tools.name: estimateSuggestTransports
tools.description: Estimate the credit cost to generate transport suggestions between two locations. Returns { realistic, min, max } credit counts.

tools.name: estimateSuggestActivities
tools.description: Estimate the credit cost to generate activity suggestions for a destination. Returns { realistic, min, max } credit counts.

tools.name: estimateSuggestAccommodations
tools.description: Estimate the credit cost to generate accommodation suggestions for a destination. Returns { realistic, min, max } credit counts.

tools.name: renameTripName
tools.description: Set or update the name of a saved trip.

name.description: The new name for the trip.

tools.name: listTopics
tools.description: Return the list of all saved news topics.

tools.name: getCurrentTopic
tools.description: Return the currently selected news topic and a summary of its latest review.

tools.name: switchTopic
tools.description: Switch the app to display a different saved topic. Use listTopics first to see available options.

topic.description: The exact topic string to switch to.

tools.name: addTopic
tools.description: Add a new topic to the saved list and switch to it.

topic.description: The news topic to add (e.g. 'Quantum Computing', 'EU Elections').

tools.name: removeTopic
tools.description: Remove a topic from the saved list.

topic.description: The exact topic string to remove.

tools.name: refreshNews
tools.description: Fetch fresh news for a topic (or the current topic if none specified). This costs credits.

topic.description: The topic to refresh. Defaults to the currently selected topic.

tools.name: navigateHistory
tools.description: Navigate backwards or forwards through the review history for the current topic.

direction.description: 'back' = older review, 'forward' = newer review.

tools.name: generateHotTopics
tools.description: Fetch a fresh list of trending hot topics across all categories (Tech, Politics, Business, Science, Entertainment, Sports). This costs credits.

tools.name: openHotTopicsModal
tools.description: Open the Hot Topics modal so the user can see the topics list.

tools.name: closeHotTopicsModal
tools.description: Close the Hot Topics modal (also stops any hot topics TTS playback).

tools.name: listHotTopics
tools.description: Return the current hot topics list organised by category, as last fetched.

tools.name: hotTopicsTtsPlay
tools.description: Open the Hot Topics modal and start or resume reading hot topic titles and reasons aloud, category by category.

tools.name: hotTopicsTtsPause
tools.description: Pause hot topics TTS playback.

tools.name: hotTopicsTtsStop
tools.description: Stop hot topics TTS playback and reset to the beginning.

tools.name: hotTopicsSkipTopic
tools.description: Skip to the next topic within the current category during hot topics TTS playback.

tools.name: hotTopicsSkipBackTopic
tools.description: Skip back to the previous topic within the current category during hot topics TTS playback.

tools.name: hotTopicsSkipBackCategory
tools.description: Skip back to the first topic of the previous category during hot topics TTS playback.

tools.name: hotTopicsSkipCategory
tools.description: Skip to the first topic of the next category during hot topics TTS playback.

tools.name: hotTopicsTtsGetState
tools.description: Return the current hot topics TTS state (idle/playing/paused), the active category index, topic index, and total categories.

tools.name: ttsPlay
tools.description: Start or resume reading the current press review aloud using text-to-speech.

tools.name: ttsPause
tools.description: Pause TTS playback.

tools.name: ttsStop
tools.description: Stop TTS playback and reset position to the beginning.

tools.name: ttsSkip
tools.description: Skip forward or backward in audio playback. Each unit = 30 seconds.

delta.description: Number of 30-second intervals to skip. Positive = forward, negative = backward.

tools.name: ttsGetState
tools.description: Return the current audio player state (idle/playing/paused), currentTime (seconds), and total duration (seconds).

tools.name: getSettings
tools.description: Return all current app settings (image toggles, etc.).

tools.name: setSetting
tools.description: Toggle or set a named app setting. Available keys: autoplay, partnershipWithReloadium.

value.description: The new value for the setting.

tools.name: getAudienceProfile
tools.description: Return the current audience profile (publisher, tone, description, ageRange, location, occupation, concerns).

tools.name: setAudienceProfile
tools.description: Update one or more audience profile fields. Available fields: publisher, tone, description, ageRange, location, occupation, concerns.

publisher.description: Name of the publishing outlet (e.g. 'TechCrunch', 'Le Monde')

location.description: Geographic focus (e.g. 'France', 'Global')

concerns.description: Key topics or concerns for the audience

tools.name: openAudienceProfileModal
tools.description: Open the Audience Profile modal so the user can view and edit their audience settings.

tools.name: getStaleTopicsCount
tools.description: Return how many saved topics have outdated news (stale) and their names. Use before calling refreshStaleTopics.

tools.name: refreshStaleTopics
tools.description: Fetch fresh news for all outdated topics at once. This costs credits (one refresh per stale topic).

tools.name: getMissingAudioCount
tools.description: Return how many topics have carousel slides but no generated audio narration yet, and their names.

tools.name: generateMissingAudio
tools.description: Generate AI narration (TTS) for all topics that have carousel slides but no audio yet. This costs credits.

tools.name: getMissingBackgroundCount
tools.description: Return how many carousel slides across all topics are missing a generated background image.

tools.name: generateMissingBackgrounds
tools.description: Generate AI background images for all carousel slides that are missing one. This costs credits.

tools.name: generateTopicAudio
tools.description: Generate AI audio narration (TTS) for a specific topic. If no topic is provided, generates for the current topic.

topic.description: The topic name to generate audio for. Omit or pass null to use the currently active topic.

tools.name: getReviewSummary
tools.description: Return the full structured review data (sections, who/what/where/when/how/why, articles list) for the current topic.

tools.name: getAppState
tools.description: Return a snapshot of the current Reloadium Clips app state: active tab, how many projects exist, and the currently active project/clip (if any).

tools.name: listClips
tools.description: Return all clips for a project (id, timing, title, quality score, processing/export status). Defaults to the currently active project if projectId is omitted.

projectId.description: Project id to list clips for. Defaults to the active project.

tools.name: getClip
tools.description: Return full details for a single clip by id, including transcript text, subtitle style, crop config, and export status. Defaults to searching the active project, then falls back to searching all projects.

projectId.description: Project id the clip belongs to (optional — will be inferred if omitted).

tools.name: switchProject
tools.description: Set the active project by id and switch to the Projects tab. Projects with a 'failed' status cannot be opened — use retryProject or deleteProject instead.

projectId.description: Project id to activate.

tools.name: switchClip
tools.description: Set the active clip by id within the currently active project (opens it in the Clip Editor).

tools.name: deleteProject
tools.description: Permanently delete a project and all of its clips by project id.

projectId.description: Project id to delete.

tools.name: deleteClip
tools.description: Permanently delete a single clip by id from a project. Defaults to the currently active project if projectId is omitted.

projectId.description: Project id the clip belongs to. Defaults to the active project.

tools.name: duplicateClip
tools.description: Duplicate a clip within the currently active project. The copy is appended to the end with '(Copy)' added to its title.

tools.name: exportClip
tools.description: Render and download a clip from the currently active project as a video file. Format defaults to 'mp4' (also supports 'zip').

format.description: Export format, defaults to 'mp4'.

tools.name: retryProject
tools.description: Retry processing a failed (or stuck) project from the beginning, optionally overriding the transcription engine.

projectId.description: Project id to retry.
